lab_title: Apparent Retrograde Motion: From Geocentric Confusion to Heliocentric Clarity
top_level_objectives: Understand why Mars appears to reverse direction in the night sky over weeks
Recognize that retrograde motion is a perspective effect arising from Earth's faster orbit overtaking Mars's slower orbit
Compare the retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and explain why outer planets loop more or less dramatically
Appreciate how the heliocentric model elegantly explains retrograde motion without requiring the complex epicycles of the geocentric model

scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the puzzle: introduce students to the observed retrograde loop of Mars as it would appear night after night from Earth's surface.
key_visuals: Starfield background showing recognizable constellations (e.g., Leo, Virgo)
Mars as a bright reddish point moving across the constellations
Sequential marker positions showing Mars's path over time: eastward drift, then westward loop, then eastward resume
Date/night labels marking the progression (e.g., 'Night 1,' 'Night 30,' 'Night 60')
student_actions: Observe Mars's position on successive nights and record its motion direction
Identify the point where Mars slows and reverses (retrograde phase begins)
Sketch or trace Mars's path on a constellation map to see the characteristic loop

scenes.brief_purpose: Show students the awkward explanation required by an Earth-centered model: Mars moving on an epicycle (a small circle riding on a larger circle) to produce the observed loop.
key_visuals: Earth fixed at the center of a circular cosmos
Mars's main deferent (large circular orbit around Earth)
Mars's epicycle (smaller circle attached to the deferent)
Animated motion showing how the epicycle's rotation produces the retrograde loop when viewed from Earth
Comparison text or overlay showing the complexity: 'Requires precise epicycle math to match observations'
student_actions: Watch the animated epicycle motion and see how it reproduces the loop
Note how many parameters (sizes, speeds, timings) must be tuned to match observations
Recognize the artificial, ad hoc nature of the model

scenes.brief_purpose: Shift to an outside (astrophysical) viewpoint and show Earth and Mars in their actual heliocentric orbits, revealing that their relative motion alone explains the retrograde loop without epicycles.
key_visuals: The Sun at the center
Earth in a small, fast orbit close to the Sun (shown in blue/white)
Mars in a larger, slower orbit farther from the Sun (shown in reddish color)
Both planets moving smoothly along their orbits with no epicycles
A projected path or 'shadow' showing what Mars would look like from Earth's viewpoint
student_actions: Observe Earth and Mars moving in their respective orbits at different speeds
Identify the moment when Earth (moving faster) begins to overtake Mars (moving slower)
Watch the projected Earth-view and confirm that the retrograde loop emerges naturally from this configuration

scenes.scene_name: The Overtaking Moment—Relative Motion in Action
scenes.brief_purpose: Zoom in on the critical phase: when Earth's faster orbit causes it to pass Mars, creating the illusion of Mars moving backward.
key_visuals: Both planets shown clearly with their orbital velocities labeled or indicated by motion vectors
A reference frame or 'relative velocity arrow' showing Mars's apparent motion as seen from Earth
Three or four snapshots of the configuration at key moments: before overtaking, during the loop, after the loop
Optional: a car-passing-car animation or analogy overlay showing the same relative motion principle
student_actions: Compare the actual motion vectors of Earth and Mars
Calculate or estimate when Earth will catch and pass Mars
Predict where in the sky (relative to background stars) the retrograde loop will appear

scenes.brief_purpose: Return to Earth's viewpoint and animate Mars's path night by night during the retrograde event, emphasizing the loop's exact shape and duration.
key_visuals: Starfield with constellations
Mars's labeled positions at regular intervals (e.g., every 3 days or every week)
The complete retrograde loop traced out with position markers and dates
Key annotations: eastward motion slowing and stopping, reversal to westward motion, resumption of eastward motion, and typical timescales (e.g., 2-month loop duration)
student_actions: Track Mars's position day by day and measure the loop's angular extent on the sky
Note the duration of the retrograde phase (roughly 2 months for Mars)
Correlate the shape and position of the loop with the heliocentric orbital configuration from the previous scenes

scenes.scene_name: Jupiter and Saturn—Retrograde Loops in Comparative Perspective
scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the model to other outer planets and show how distance from the Sun affects the retrograde loop's size and shape.
key_visuals: Heliocentric view showing the Sun, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn in their respective orbits (to scale or clearly labeled)
Retrograde loops for each planet shown side by side or in separate subpanels, with Jupiter's loop smaller than Mars's and Saturn's loop even smaller
Orbital velocity indicators or speed labels for each planet
Text annotations showing orbital periods (Mars ~2 years, Jupiter ~12 years, Saturn ~29 years)
student_actions: Observe why Jupiter's retrograde loop is smaller and less dramatic than Mars's (Jupiter is farther from the Sun, relative velocity is smaller)
Predict Saturn's retrograde behavior based on its even greater distance and slower motion
Compare the actual loop sizes and durations across the three planets

scenes.brief_purpose: Pull together the key insight: the heliocentric model explains all retrograde motion as a simple consequence of relative orbital motion, requiring no epicycles or special mechanisms.
key_visuals: Side-by-side or toggle view showing geocentric epicycles versus heliocentric simple orbits for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn
A summary diagram or infographic showing the relationship: relative orbital speed → loop size and speed
A timeline or flowchart indicating how observations of retrograde motion drove the shift from geocentrism to heliocentrism
student_actions: Articulate why the heliocentric model is simpler and more powerful
Explain retrograde motion qualitatively using only orbital mechanics (no epicycles)
Discuss why historical astronomers found the geocentric model plausible despite its complexity, and what would have motivated a paradigm shift

scenes.scene_name: Challenge—Predicting Retrograde Events and Testing Understanding
scenes.brief_purpose: Apply understanding to new scenarios: predict when the next retrograde event will occur and whether a hypothetical planet would show retrograde motion.
key_visuals: Interactive orbital configuration tool or controls allowing students to adjust orbital parameters (semimajor axis, orbital period, or current positions)
Animated projection showing the predicted Earth-view as parameters change
Question prompts displayed on screen
student_actions: Use orbital parameters to predict the next Mars retrograde event (or Jupiter retrograde event)
Adjust a hypothetical planet's distance and predict whether and how dramatically it would exhibit retrograde motion
Reason about whether an interior planet (like Venus) would ever show retrograde motion as seen from Earth, and explain why or why not
